title: AI Concept Classifier Quiz
description: Test your ability to classify Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning concepts into the correct category. Covers the full H63AIS curriculum from data preprocessing to deep learning architectures.

config.instructionText: Select the correct category for this concept

scenarios.scenario: A technique that computes the partial derivatives of the loss function with respect to each weight by propagating errors backward from the output layer through hidden layers using the chain rule.
scenarios.explanation: Backpropagation is a core neural network training mechanism. While it involves optimization concepts (gradient computation), it is fundamentally a neural network algorithm that computes error signals layer by layer using the chain rule.
scenarios.hint: Think about which layer-by-layer process is unique to training multi-layer networks.

scenarios.scenario: You split your dataset into three parts: 70% for training the model, 15% for tuning hyperparameters, and 15% for final performance assessment on unseen data.
scenarios.explanation: Data splitting into training, validation, and test sets is a data preprocessing step. It happens before model training begins and determines how data flows through the ML pipeline.
scenarios.hint: This step prepares data before any model is trained.

scenarios.scenario: An algorithm that classifies a new data point by finding the K closest data points in the training set and assigning the class that appears most frequently among those neighbors.
scenarios.explanation: K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) is a classification algorithm. It uses distance metrics and majority voting among the K nearest training examples to predict the class of a new instance. Unlike clustering, it requires labeled training data.
scenarios.hint: This is a supervised method that uses labeled data and distance measurements.

scenarios.scenario: A specialized neural network layer that slides a small matrix (e.g., 3x3) across an input image, computing element-wise multiplications and summing the results to produce a feature map.
scenarios.explanation: The convolution operation with filters/kernels is a defining component of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), which fall under Deep Learning Architectures. While it involves matrix operations, the concept is specific to CNN architecture design.
scenarios.hint: This operation is the defining component of a specific deep learning architecture for images.

scenarios.scenario: Instead of computing the gradient over the entire training set, you randomly select a single training example at each step to compute the gradient and update the parameters.
scenarios.explanation: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is an optimization algorithm. It is a variant of gradient descent that uses one random sample per iteration, trading accuracy of the gradient estimate for faster computation per step.
scenarios.hint: This is a variant of a well-known parameter update strategy.

scenarios.scenario: A table that shows four counts: how many positive examples were correctly predicted (TP), how many were missed (FN), how many negatives were incorrectly flagged (FP), and how many negatives were correctly identified (TN).
scenarios.explanation: The confusion matrix is a model evaluation tool. It summarizes classification performance by counting true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives, forming the basis for metrics like precision, recall, and F1 score.
scenarios.hint: This is a tool for measuring how well a trained model performs.

scenarios.scenario: An unsupervised algorithm that partitions data into K groups by iteratively assigning each point to the nearest center, then recalculating centers as the mean of assigned points until convergence.
scenarios.explanation: K-Means is a clustering algorithm. It groups unlabeled data into K clusters by minimizing the distance between points and their assigned centroids. Unlike classification, it discovers structure in data without predefined labels.
scenarios.hint: This algorithm works with unlabeled data to discover natural groupings.

scenarios.scenario: A model that predicts a continuous output value y by computing y = w1*x1 + w2*x2 + ... + wn*xn + b, where the parameters w and b are learned by minimizing the sum of squared differences between predictions and actual values.
scenarios.explanation: This describes linear regression: a model that fits a linear equation to data by minimizing squared loss. The normal equation or gradient descent can solve for the optimal parameters w and b.
scenarios.hint: This model predicts continuous values using a weighted sum of features.

scenarios.scenario: A collection of over 14 million labeled images spanning more than 20,000 categories, created by Li Fei-Fei's team and widely used as a benchmark for training and evaluating computer vision models.
scenarios.explanation: ImageNet is a benchmark dataset, which falls under Data Acquisition. It is a resource for obtaining labeled training data, not a model architecture or evaluation technique. Its creation was a data collection and annotation effort.
scenarios.hint: Think about where datasets themselves fit in the ML pipeline.

scenarios.scenario: A function that squashes any real-valued input into the range (0, 1), computed as f(x) = 1 / (1 + e^(-x)). It is used to convert raw model outputs into probabilities for binary classification.
scenarios.explanation: The sigmoid function is central to logistic regression and binary classification. While it also appears as a neural network activation function, its primary conceptual role in this course is converting linear outputs into class probabilities for classification tasks.
scenarios.hint: This function converts outputs into probabilities for a two-class problem.

scenarios.scenario: The process of detecting and handling records with empty fields in a dataset, using strategies such as deletion of incomplete rows, mean/median imputation, or model-based imputation before training.
scenarios.explanation: Handling missing values is a core data preprocessing task. It involves cleaning the dataset so that models can be trained effectively, occurring after data acquisition but before model training.
scenarios.hint: This happens after you have the data but before you train any model.

scenarios.scenario: When a model performs very well on training data (low training error) but poorly on new, unseen data (high validation error), indicating it has memorized noise rather than learning the underlying pattern.
scenarios.explanation: Overfitting is a model evaluation concept. It describes a gap between training and validation performance, indicating poor generalization. Detecting and addressing overfitting is fundamental to evaluating model quality.
scenarios.hint: This describes a discrepancy between training and validation performance.

scenarios.scenario: An operation where each element in one matrix row is multiplied with the corresponding element in a matrix column, and the results are summed to produce a single entry in the output matrix.
scenarios.explanation: Matrix multiplication is a fundamental linear algebra operation. While it underpins many ML algorithms (regression, neural networks), the concept itself belongs to the mathematical foundations category.
scenarios.hint: This is a pure mathematical operation that many ML algorithms depend on.

scenarios.scenario: A density-based algorithm that groups together points in high-density regions and marks points in low-density regions as noise. It requires two parameters: epsilon (neighborhood radius) and MinPts (minimum points).
scenarios.explanation: DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) is a clustering algorithm. Unlike K-Means, it can find arbitrarily shaped clusters and automatically identifies noise points without requiring the number of clusters in advance.
scenarios.hint: This unsupervised algorithm discovers groups based on point density.

scenarios.scenario: A technique that adds a penalty term (lambda times the sum of squared weights) to the loss function, discouraging large parameter values to prevent the model from fitting noise in the training data.
scenarios.explanation: L2 regularization (Ridge) is an optimization technique. By adding a penalty term to the objective function, it constrains the optimization process to prefer simpler models, helping prevent overfitting during training.
scenarios.hint: This modifies the loss function to control model complexity during training.

scenarios.scenario: A type of neural network that processes sequential data by maintaining a hidden state vector that is updated at each time step, allowing information from earlier inputs to influence later predictions.
scenarios.explanation: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are a deep learning architecture designed for sequential data. They extend basic neural network concepts with recurrent connections that maintain temporal information across time steps.
scenarios.hint: This architecture is specifically designed for data that has a temporal or sequential order.

scenarios.scenario: A neuron that takes multiple weighted inputs, sums them with a bias, and applies an activation function. If the result exceeds a threshold, it outputs 1; otherwise it outputs 0. This is the simplest model of a biological neuron.
scenarios.explanation: The perceptron is a foundational neural network concept. It is the simplest artificial neuron model, consisting of weighted inputs, a bias, and a step activation function. It forms the building block of all neural networks.
scenarios.hint: This is the most basic building block that all neural networks are made of.

scenarios.scenario: You have a set of features with very different scales: age ranges from 0-100, salary from 20000-200000, and rating from 1-5. You transform all features to the range [0, 1] before feeding them into a model.
scenarios.explanation: Data normalization (min-max scaling) is a data preprocessing step. Rescaling features to a common range prevents features with larger magnitudes from dominating the learning process.
scenarios.hint: This transformation is applied to data before training to ensure fair treatment of all features.

scenarios.scenario: A plot that shows the trade-off between the True Positive Rate and the False Positive Rate at various classification thresholds. The area under this curve summarizes overall classifier performance.
scenarios.explanation: The ROC curve and AUC are model evaluation tools. They provide a threshold-independent way to assess classifier performance, showing how sensitivity and specificity trade off across all possible decision thresholds.
scenarios.hint: This visualization is used to assess and compare trained classifiers.

scenarios.scenario: A probability distribution that describes the likelihood of a continuous random variable, characterized by its mean (mu) and standard deviation (sigma), forming the familiar bell-shaped curve.
scenarios.explanation: The Gaussian (normal) distribution is a mathematical foundation concept. It is a probability distribution used throughout ML for assumptions about data, noise, and maximum likelihood estimation.
scenarios.hint: This is a mathematical concept from probability theory, not a specific ML algorithm.

scenarios.scenario: The process of manually or programmatically assigning correct labels (such as 'cat' or 'dog') to raw data samples so they can be used to train supervised learning models.
scenarios.explanation: Data annotation is a data acquisition activity. It involves creating the labels that supervised learning requires. This happens during the data collection phase, before any preprocessing or model training begins.
scenarios.hint: This creates the ground truth labels needed before any model can learn.

scenarios.scenario: A layer in a CNN that reduces the spatial dimensions of feature maps by selecting the maximum value in each local region (e.g., 2x2 window), decreasing computation while retaining important features.
scenarios.explanation: Max pooling is a component of CNN architecture (Deep Learning Architectures). It is a downsampling operation specific to convolutional neural networks that reduces spatial dimensions while preserving the most prominent features.
scenarios.hint: This is a specific operation within a particular deep learning architecture for images.

scenarios.scenario: A hyperparameter that controls how large each step is when updating model parameters in the direction of the negative gradient. If too large, the model may overshoot; if too small, training is very slow.
scenarios.explanation: The learning rate is an optimization concept. It controls the step size during gradient descent, directly affecting whether and how quickly the optimization converges to a good solution.
scenarios.hint: This controls the size of parameter updates during the training process.

scenarios.scenario: A function that takes a vector of real numbers and normalizes it into a probability distribution where all outputs sum to 1, commonly used in the final layer for multi-class classification problems.
scenarios.explanation: The softmax function is a classification concept. It generalizes the sigmoid function to multiple classes, converting raw scores into class probabilities. It is the standard output transformation for multi-class classification tasks.
scenarios.hint: This function produces probabilities for problems with more than two classes.

scenarios.scenario: An advanced RNN architecture that uses three gates (input, forget, and output) to control information flow, solving the vanishing gradient problem and enabling the network to learn long-range dependencies in sequences.
scenarios.explanation: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) is a deep learning architecture. It extends the basic RNN with gating mechanisms that control what information to remember, forget, and output, enabling learning from long sequences.
scenarios.hint: This is a specialized variant of a sequential deep learning model with gating mechanisms.

scenarios.scenario: You use a Python library to create a scatter plot of two features from your dataset, colored by class label, to visually check whether the classes are separable before building a classifier.
scenarios.explanation: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is part of data preprocessing. Visualizing feature distributions and class separability helps understand the data before selecting and training a model. It informs preprocessing and modeling decisions.
scenarios.hint: This visual exploration happens before model training to understand the data.

scenarios.scenario: A closed-form solution that directly computes the optimal weight vector for a linear model by solving w = (X^T X)^(-1) X^T y, avoiding the need for iterative optimization.
scenarios.explanation: The normal equation is a linear regression concept. It provides a direct analytical solution for the optimal parameters of a linear regression model, as opposed to using iterative methods like gradient descent.
scenarios.hint: This formula gives the exact optimal solution for a specific type of model.

scenarios.scenario: A metric that measures the proportion of positive predictions that were actually correct. It answers: of all the items the model labeled as positive, how many truly were positive?
scenarios.explanation: Precision is a model evaluation metric. It measures the accuracy of positive predictions (TP / (TP + FP)). Along with recall and F1 score, it provides a nuanced view of classifier performance beyond simple accuracy.
scenarios.hint: This is a metric computed after training to judge prediction quality.

scenarios.scenario: A nonlinear activation function defined as f(x) = max(0, x) that outputs zero for negative inputs and passes positive inputs unchanged. It is the most widely used activation in modern deep networks.
scenarios.explanation: ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) is a neural network activation function. It is a fundamental building block used across all types of neural networks, from simple fully connected networks to deep CNNs and RNNs.
scenarios.hint: This is a core component used inside neurons across many network types.

scenarios.scenario: Applying random transformations such as rotation, flipping, cropping, and color jittering to existing training images to artificially increase the size and diversity of the training dataset.
scenarios.explanation: Data augmentation is a data acquisition technique. It generates new training samples from existing ones through transformations, effectively expanding the dataset. This addresses the challenge of limited training data availability.
scenarios.hint: This technique creates more training data from what you already have.

incorrect: Not quite -- now you know for next time!

Learning from mistakes makes us better!

categoryDescriptions.Neural Networks: Perceptron, activation functions, fully connected networks, forward pass, backpropagation, and training loop concepts
categoryDescriptions.Deep Learning Architectures: CNN layers and operations, RNN/LSTM, advanced architectures, and model deployment
categoryDescriptions.Optimization: Gradient descent variants, learning rate, convergence, regularization, and parameter update strategies
categoryDescriptions.Model Evaluation: Regression and classification metrics, confusion matrix, ROC/AUC, overfitting, and model selection
categoryDescriptions.Classification: Logistic regression, sigmoid/softmax, KNN, binary and multi-class classification, and decision boundaries
categoryDescriptions.Clustering: K-Means, DBSCAN, centroids, density concepts, and unsupervised grouping algorithms
categoryDescriptions.Data Preprocessing: Data cleaning, normalization, feature engineering, splitting, and exploratory analysis
categoryDescriptions.Data Acquisition: Dataset collection, annotation, benchmark datasets, data augmentation, and data sources
categoryDescriptions.Linear Regression: Linear models, loss functions, normal equation, slope, intercept, and residuals
categoryDescriptions.Linear Algebra and Math: Matrix operations, probability distributions, and statistical foundations

endScreen.tipsTitle: Tips for Better AI Concept Classification:
tips: Ask whether the concept is about preparing data, building a model, or evaluating results.
Distinguish between general neural network concepts and specific deep learning architectures (CNN, RNN, LSTM).
Remember: optimization is about HOW parameters are updated; evaluation is about HOW WELL the model performs.

excellent.subMessage: You have an excellent understanding of AI/ML concept categories.

good.subMessage: You classified most AI concepts correctly. Review the explanations for the ones you missed.

fair.subMessage: Keep studying the relationships between AI/ML topics to improve.

needsWork.subMessage: Review the course taxonomy and try again. Practice makes perfect.
